title: Trump: New York Attorney General and Trump enemy Letitia James indicted
description_short: Trump: New York Attorney General and Trump enemy Letitia James indicted
description_medium: A federal grand jury in Virginia indicted New York Attorney General Letitia James on October 9, 2025, on bank-fraud and false-statement charges. Prosecutors alleged that she misrepresented a Norfolk, Virginia, home in seeking mortgage terms. The indictment followed a Justice Department subpoena in August related to an investigation linked to her civil-fraud case against Trump. The charges remain allegations, not findings of guilt.
description_long:
On October 9, 2025, a federal grand jury in Virginia indicted New York Attorney General Letitia James. Prosecutors charged her with bank fraud and making false statements to a financial institution. The allegations concern a Norfolk, Virginia, home: the administration alleged that James represented it as a second residence to obtain more favorable mortgage terms and rented it to a family. James denied wrongdoing. An indictment is an accusation, not a verdict.

Two months earlier, the Justice Department had subpoenaed James in an investigation linked to her civil-fraud case against Trump. That subpoena and the October indictment were distinct steps. James had sued Trump as New York attorney general, and she accused him of using the law to retaliate against her. The case’s eventual result must be established from later court records; the charges remain allegations rather than findings of guilt.
organization_tags: Office of the New York Attorney General

title: Trump admin cuts mental health jobs during shutdown
description_short: Trump admin cuts mental health jobs during shutdown
description_medium: During the second week of the 2025 federal shutdown, the administration laid off roughly 125 employees at the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration, according to the linked report. SAMHSA supports mental-health and addiction services, including the 988 crisis lifeline. An NPR source described staff as shocked and unsure why the cuts were happening. The account does not document a service interruption.
description_long:
During the second week of the 2025 federal shutdown, the Trump administration laid off roughly 125 employees at the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration, NPR reported. SAMHSA is the federal agency responsible for work on mental-health and substance-use services. It oversees the 988 suicide and crisis lifeline and issues grants for mental-health and addiction programs; before the layoffs, it employed about 900 people.

An NPR source described the mood among affected staff as shock and said they did not understand why the cuts were occurring. The report does not identify the employees’ positions, say whether the separations were temporary or permanent, or name programs that lost staff. It also provides no evidence that the 988 service stopped operating. The layoffs reduced a sizeable share of SAMHSA’s workforce during the shutdown, but their effect on particular services remains unspecified.
organization_tags: Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration

title: Trump takes federal control over three Washington D.C. golf courses
description_short: Trump takes federal control over three Washington D.C. golf courses
description_medium: On December 30, 2025, the Interior Department ended the National Links Trust’s lease to manage three Washington, D.C., municipal golf courses, returning their operation to federal control. The nonprofit had held a 50-year lease for about five years. The administration said the trust was in default but offered no evidence for that claim, according to the reporting. Planned renovation work stopped, while the courses remained open at the time.
description_long:
On December 30, 2025, the Trump administration, acting through the Interior Department, terminated the National Links Trust’s lease to manage and renovate Rock Creek, East Potomac and Langston golf courses in Washington, D.C. The National Park Service owns the land. The nonprofit had held a 50-year lease for about five years, with a mission of making golf more accessible to the public.

The administration said the trust was in default but offered no evidence for that assertion. The termination returned operational control of the three municipal courses to the federal government. The courses remained open at the time, but long-term renovation projects stopped, leaving future management and planned improvements uncertain. Trump had announced an intention to redo the courses earlier that month. The lease termination therefore changed who controlled the facilities and interrupted work already planned for them; its eventual effect on public access and the final renovation plan remained unresolved.

title: Trump FBI raids home of Washington Post reporter
description_short: Trump FBI raids home of Washington Post reporter
description_medium: On January 14, 2026, FBI agents searched Washington Post reporter Hannah Natanson’s Virginia home under a warrant. They told her she was not the subject of a criminal investigation and said they were seeking information about Maryland system administrator Aurelio Perez-Lugones, who was suspected of mishandling classified material. Agents searched Natanson’s phone, two laptops and a Garmin watch.
description_long:
The FBI executed a search warrant at Washington Post reporter Hannah Natanson’s Virginia home on January 14, 2026. Agents told Natanson she was not the subject of a criminal investigation and said they were seeking information about Maryland system administrator Aurelio Perez-Lugones. Court documents reportedly alleged that Perez-Lugones mishandled classified information related to an unspecified country; intelligence reports said documents were found in his lunchbox and basement.

Agents searched Natanson’s phone, personal laptop, a laptop issued by the Post and a Garmin watch. The search reached a reporter’s personal and work devices while investigators pursued information about another person. Attorney General Pam Bondi had removed a prior policy limiting searches of reporters’ phone records. The Privacy Protection Act still restricts searches of journalists’ work materials in many circumstances, according to the reporting. The article does not describe the warrant’s precise limits or the legal process used to protect reporting materials.

title: Trump: Greg Bovino demoted. Tom Homan deployed to Minneapolis amid carnage
description_short: Trump: Greg Bovino demoted. Tom Homan deployed to Minneapolis amid carnage
description_medium: On January 26, 2026, Trump said border czar Tom Homan would go to Minneapolis after calls with Governor Tim Walz and Mayor Jacob Frey. The announcement came during controversy over federal immigration operations and after the fatal shootings of Renee Nicole Good and Alex Pretti by federal agents. Border Patrol commander Greg Bovino was set to leave the city and was removed from his operational role, according to the linked timeline.
description_long:
On January 26, 2026, Donald Trump announced that border czar Tom Homan would go to Minneapolis after speaking with Minnesota Governor Tim Walz and Mayor Jacob Frey. Frey told Trump that the disruption caused by federal agents was unsustainable, according to the linked account. The same day, Border Patrol commander Gregory Bovino and other federal agents were expected to leave the city by the following day; Bovino was removed from his role leading Operation At Large.

Bovino also lost access to official government social-media accounts. The Department of Homeland Security denied that he had been fired, and the account said he was expected to transfer to El Centro, California, to resume overseeing Customs and Border Protection operations there. The personnel changes followed fatal shootings of Renee Nicole Good and Alex Pretti by federal agents and intense criticism of immigration enforcement in Minneapolis. Trump’s announcement identified a new official to oversee the response, but the available account does not provide Homan’s written orders or establish whether the operation’s tactics changed.

title: Trump: US claims ‘emergency refugee situation’ as it admits 10,000 more white South Africans
description_short: Trump: US claims ‘emergency refugee situation’ as it admits 10,000 more white South Africans
description_medium: US claims ‘emergency refugee situation’ as it admits 10,000 more white South Africans. Trump has repeatedly made false claims that white Afrikaners facing genocide with costs of resettling them at $100m This entry is cataloged as a standalone event because it captures a concrete action, public statement, legal development, documented relationship, or policy consequence linked directly or indirectly to Trump. The downstream effects include institutional stress, public-trust erosion, and accountability pressure across affected systems.
description_long:
In May 2026, the U.S. government said it would raise the number of white South Africans admitted through its refugee program that year from about 7,500 to 17,500. Officials described “unforeseen developments in South Africa” as creating an emergency refugee situation. The increase added 10,000 places to the announced annual total.

The policy was presented amid repeated claims by Donald Trump that white Afrikaners faced racial persecution and “white genocide.” The Guardian reported that those genocide claims were false and that South Africa’s government had strongly rejected them. The refugee-admission decision is a policy action, while the genocide language is a separate claim about conditions in South Africa. The announcement set a higher admissions target but did not describe each applicant’s circumstances or eligibility. That increase more than doubled the earlier target, and the new limit applies to the current refugee program year.

title: 22 Courts Reject Trump DOJ Voter Roll Seizure Crusade
description_short: 22 Courts Reject Trump DOJ Voter Roll Seizure Crusade
description_medium: Twenty-one federal district courts and one federal appeals court have now rejected the Trump DOJ's attempt to seize unredacted state voter registration databases containing Social Security numbers, driver's licenses, and full birthdates. Judges appointed by presidents of both parties — including 8 Trump appointees — ruled the DOJ misinterpreted a Jim Crow-era civil rights law to justify mass voter data collection. Despite a 0-22 record, the DOJ continues filing identical legal arguments in remaining states.
description_long:
The Justice Department sought Maryland’s unredacted statewide voter file, including dates of birth, addresses, driver’s-license numbers and partial Social Security numbers. U.S. District Judge Stephanie Gallagher dismissed the department’s lawsuit. She concluded that the federal government had not shown the voter list was a record Maryland had to produce under the law it cited.

The department relied on the Civil Rights Act of 1960. Gallagher reasoned that the government’s reading would conflict with election laws requiring states to update their voter lists. She wrote that the act did not require Maryland to turn over the complete file. The decision joined rulings against similar requests in other states. The Associated Press reported that, after the Maryland decision in June 2026, the department had lost similar cases in nine states; it had sued in 30 states and the District of Columbia. The Maryland dispute concerned federal access to sensitive voter information and the legal authority for demanding it.

title: Rubio says Iran's economy is in shambles while leaving the door open to diplomacy
description_short: Rubio says Iran's economy is in shambles while leaving the door open to diplomacy
description_medium: In July 19 remarks, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Iran's economy was 'in shambles,' cited severe inflation and shortages, and said a diplomatic opening would be positive if Iranian factions favoring negotiations gained influence. Separate reporting shows the June U.S.-Iran MOU later broke down and hostilities resumed. The record should not state as fact that Rubio personally admitted a two-week violation or that he 'could not articulate an endgame' without a direct source.
description_long:
On July 19, 2026, Secretary of State Marco Rubio described Iran’s economy as “in shambles,” citing severe inflation and shortages of essential goods. He said an opening for diplomacy would be positive if Iranian factions that favored negotiations gained influence. His remarks focused on economic strain inside Iran and the possibility that its internal politics could create room for talks.

The comments came after a U.S.–Iran memorandum of understanding was announced in June. Reuters reported that the agreement was intended to halt the conflict and frame follow-on talks. By July, news coverage described disputes about its implementation, and hostilities had resumed. Rubio’s public remarks addressed diplomacy as a possibility but did not lay out how the conflict would end or resolve the agreement’s status. The distinction between his July comments and the separate memorandum matters: the remarks documented Iran’s economic pressure and conditional openness to talks, while the agreement’s breakdown was a separate development.

title: Trump Media Sells 100K Monthly Subscription for Early Truth Social Access
description_short: Trump Media Sells 100K Monthly Subscription for Early Truth Social Access
description_medium: Trump Media said it had signed more than 10 customer agreements for Truth API, a paid feed of Truth Social posts aimed mainly at high-frequency trading firms. The reported contracts cost between $60,000 and $100,000 per month. The feed delivers public posts directly to subscribers’ systems, giving traders a potential speed advantage over people using the public app. The reporting does not establish that subscribers traded on particular posts.
description_long:
Trump Media & Technology Group said in an August 2026 earnings call that it had signed more than 10 customer agreements for Truth API, a paid data feed of Truth Social posts. The company said most customers were high-frequency trading firms and that contracts generally cost between $60,000 and $100,000 per month. The feed sends posts directly to customer systems; CNN reported that this can give Wall Street traders a head start over users who see posts through the public app. It also carries posts from other leading Truth Social accounts, not only Donald Trump’s.

Trump often uses the platform to announce policies and other developments that can move markets. A faster feed gives subscribers a potential trading advantage and raises questions about the president’s media company selling quicker access to posts he publishes. Trump Media said the posts are public and defended the service. The reporting did not identify trades made by subscribers in response to particular posts. The company’s disclosure established the customer agreements and price range, while actual trading effects remained unknown.

preserved_fields.description_short: Trump Media Sells 100K Monthly Subscription for Early Truth Social Access
